title: Too late
hook: Pharaoh believes as he drowns, and his body is kept as a sign (10:90–92)

segments.voice: Yesterday: wali, the friends of God, who believe and are mindful. Your line was no fear, no grief.

The sea has opened, and a people who were slaves in Egypt are walking through it on dry ground. Behind them, chariots. Pharaoh and his army have chased them to the water's edge and, with the whole might of Egypt behind them, ridden straight in after them. The Qur'an tells this crossing in several surahs. Surah Yunus stops on a single moment: the water closing over Pharaoh's head, and Pharaoh finally saying the words Musa had been asking him to say.

Verse ninety, in paraphrase: when drowning overtook him, Pharaoh said, I believe that there is no god but the one the Children of Israel believe in, and I am of those who submit. Notice the words: I am of the muslimin, those who submit. The right sentence; almost a creed. And the answer comes in verse ninety-one: Now? When you rebelled before, and were among the corrupters? It's not that the words were wrong. It's when they came. Again and again Musa brought signs: a staff, a hand, a flood, locusts, frogs, blood. Each time Pharaoh promised, and each time he went back. Only with water in his throat did he say it, and by then it wasn't a choice anymore, only a sight he couldn't deny. A hadith reported by at-Tirmidhi says God accepts a servant's repentance until the death rattle reaches the throat. The door stays open a long time. But not forever. Then verse ninety-two, in Pickthall's translation: "But this day We save thee in thy body that thou mayst be a portent for those after thee." His body is kept, a sign for whoever comes later. Which Pharaoh was it? The Qur'an doesn't say, and neither does the Bible's telling in Exodus. Some modern writers link the verse to preserved royal bodies in Egyptian museums; historians have not settled who the Pharaoh of the exodus was, or whether one can be named at all. What the verse keeps is the timing. The right words, too late, become a warning rather than a rescue.
screen: `I BELIEVE — AS THE WATER CLOSES.` · `NOW? WHEN YOU REBELLED BEFORE?` · `THE DOOR OPEN UNTIL THE LAST BREATH.` · `HIS BODY KEPT AS A SIGN.` · then, large: `DON'T WAIT FOR THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Think of a right thing you've been putting off: an apology, a phone call to someone getting old, a debt, a visit. Picture it clearly, then picture its smallest possible version, a text that starts the apology, a date in the calendar for the visit. If you pray, you can ask for help not to wait.
Too late. Pharaoh says the right words only as the sea closes over him, and the answer comes: now? Today's word.
Your line: don't wait for the water. The right words matter most while there's still a choice. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers use Pharaoh's last words in 10:90–92 to teach that repentance should come while there is still a choice, alongside the hadith that God accepts repentance until the death rattle.

fork.setup: you've seen sign after sign for years and promised each time to change. now the water is at your throat. what does the Qur'an say about believing now?
options: better late than never; it's accepted.
fork.reveal: now? when you rebelled before? the words were right; the time for choosing them had passed.

original.note: Arabic: "now?" the one-word answer to Pharaoh in 10:91.

trapdoor: what you thought: a villain finally gets what he deserves.
what it means: the right words only count while they're still a choice; Pharaoh waited until they weren't.
what a scholar hears: 10:90 has Pharaoh call himself one of al-muslimin; at-Tirmidhi's hadith sets the limit of repentance at the death rattle (al-gharghara).

chat.says: If Pharaoh finally said he believed, why does the story treat it as a warning?
options: He said it only as he drowned, after years of signs; the answer was: now?
He never actually said he believed; he only cried out to Musa for help.
The story is mainly about Musa's patience, not about Pharaoh's words.
chat.meaning: Verse ninety-one answers his words: now, when you rebelled before? The words were right; the time for choosing them had passed.

at-Tirmidhi.meaning: compiler of a major hadith collection

Exodus.meaning: the Bible's book that tells the crossing of the sea
